query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) based on tungsten and its refractory counterparts (for example, variants in the Nb–Mo–Ta–W family) will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition with temperature because its complex, distorted lattice and hierarchical microstructure resist the conventional temper embrittlement seen in single‐principal‐element alloys. In a moderate intermediate temperature range, an emergent mechanism (such as interface decohesion or activation of less-mobile phases) can temporarily reduce ductility before the activation of additional slip systems and diffusion‐aided deformation restores ductility at higher temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy in its processed (e.g., as-cast or HPHT-treated) state with a hierarchical two-phase or dual‐lamella microstructure and predominantly ductile behavior at low temperature.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to a controlled temperature ramp spanning from low (room or moderately low) temperatures through an intermediate narrow temperature window to high temperatures.
generation.conditions: The experiment is conducted under inert atmosphere or vacuum to avoid oxidation, with temperature changes performed slowly enough to allow microstructural evolution. Mechanical tests (e.g., tensile testing) are carried out at discrete temperature points to capture changes.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces and a distribution of local lattice distortions created by the multiple principal refractory elements.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, dislocation-mediated plasticity and ductile behavior predominate. As temperature increases into an intermediate window, subtle changes (for example, slight decohesion at certain interfaces or activation of less-mobile phases) reduce ductility, producing a brittle response similar to temper embrittlement. At even higher temperatures, activation of additional slip systems and enhanced atomic diffusion reintroduce ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A clear ductile–brittle–ductile transition will be observed: high ductility at low temperatures, a pronounced drop in ductility over a narrow intermediate temperature range, and recovery of ductility at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties (e.g., tensile ductility, yield strength) measured at room temperature prior to temperature ramping.
generation.boundary: The transition is expected only within a specific, narrow intermediate temperature range and may depend on alloy composition and processing history; the effect may not be observed if the microstructural features (e.g., phase distribution and interface coherency) are significantly altered.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature intervals for the brittle regime, the magnitude of the drop in ductility, and the sensitivity to compositional variations in the alloy are not precisely established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy and subject them to a controlled temperature ramp test. At pre-determined temperature intervals (covering low, intermediate, and high ranges), perform mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests) and microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM) to monitor ductility changes and structural evolution.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy does not show a statistically significant drop in ductility in a narrow temperature range (i.e., a ductile–brittle–ductile transition) or if microstructural analyses fail to reveal the expected changes (such as changes in interface coherency or activation of distinct deformation mechanisms), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).
